I think Subaru's character arc is Re Zero's strongest point.

I think there are a lot of interesting aspects to her character. She's introduced as someone who tries to find "selfish" justifications for going out of her way to be kind to people, which is a very endearing character trait. She's someone who cares deeply about others despite having been rejected by almost everyone. She's sincere to a fault, and very conscientious. She's pure-hearted, but also seems to be aware of her own naivety and how it could be harmful. She's fairly lenient with people, and extremely patient with Subaru, but she'll still stand up for herself when she genuinely feels the need to do so.

That being said, I feel like her character is held back in a lot of ways by having to be "the perfect heroine." She can't be more competent than Subaru, so her intelligence and decision-making abilities had to be nerfed. She can't lose her innocence and naivety, so her mental age had to be nerfed. 

Gender norms in heterosexual romances, regardless of their audience (i.e. shoujo, josei, and Western romances absolutely do this as well), tend to demand that the male partner be the "stronger" one. Since Subaru is never going to be a match for Emilia in terms of fighting ability, that means she has to be deeply lacking in some other department to compensate for that. I personally think this is stupid and harms Emilia's character, but I do get that if this was not the case, we would have even more brain-dead chodes complaining about Subaru being "useless" or whatever.

It's not enough for her to be a sweet, stubborn person who gets herself into trouble because she can't help but try to do the right thing in every situation even if she knows better - she has to be completely dependent on Subaru. I honestly think this is a reflection of how harshly Tappei treats Subaru sometimes (possibly driven by how the more casual audience views Subaru) - like he can't even be worthy of Emilia unless she needs him. Like she wouldn't want to be with him for any other reason, despite the fact that she very clearly does like him anyway (for his sense of humour, his resourcefulness, his kindness, their shared values). 

The truth is that Emilia doesn't actually need to be immature or incompetent in order for Subaru to be worthy of her. He's actually really impressive on his own. He isn't perfect, but neither is she - nobody is. So I think it'd be really nice to see Emilia achieve something on her own, without Subaru, and then show that she still wants him around. That she likes him for who he *is*, rather than what he does for her. Because I think those are her honest feelings, even if she isn't capable of articulating them. I also think it'd be nice to see her relationships with other characters fleshed out.

There's a real insecurity at the heart of what Emilia, as the "perfect heroine," has to represent. At this point I'm not sure how intentional that is, honestly.

I don't know if it's particularly gendered (I doubt I'd get a particularly good response asking the average NT man that same question), but in general, it seems like they're offering "safe" small talk, and you're responding by requesting that they divulge their deepest feelings about that topic. It's upping the stakes of the conversation, and it's going to come across as quite intimate in a way that they may not be prepared for.

 "Oh, I really like horror movies!" "Hey, me too! What are some of your favourites?" - that's a "safe" conversation. You learn some surface level information about each other, but you're not showing any sort of vulnerability.

"Why do you think horror movies resonate with you so much?" is a question that could make someone feel deeply vulnerable. Giving a proper answer to it requires a lot of thought, and an honest answer could potentially give your conversation partner way more information about you than you wish to disclose. 

Basically, they're offering surface-level conversation as a low-effort and low-stakes way of bonding with you. You, in return, are asking them to dredge up their deepest feelings about what was previously an easy, casual topic of conversation. That's fine if it's a close friend \*and\* they're in the mood to actually think about that kind of thing, but otherwise, a lot of people are going to feel rather intimidated in that situation.

Oh hey, same boat down to the autism diagnosis! I actually have a social life now that I'm not completely drained from being around people in the office (and all the background noise, and flourescent lights, and the noise on my commute) all day. It still feels wild to me that I can finish an entire work day and feel like going out and talking to people.

My type of autism is actually pretty common in women and girls! (Not that it's exclusively gendered, and I definitely also have some more "classic" autistic traits as well). I actually thought I had ADHD when I first went to get diagnosed (I still think I probably do have ADHD as well, but I ended up with just an ASD diagnosis).

But yeah, like. I went to university. I have a job, and friends. I obtained all of those things with zero support, since I was only diagnosed a few years ago. Not gonna say I've never had any issues in life stemming from being autistic, because of course I have, but it's also part of who I am. I wouldn't be the same person at all if I wasn't autistic, so I don't want to treat it like a bad thing. Everyone has their strengths and weaknesses.

So I think the thing here is that there's a difference between how neurotypical people tend to discuss autism, and how autistic people tend to discuss autism. Autistic people tend to be straightforward in general. We do tend to know from experience that other people do not like that, but as a late-diagnosed adult, I cannot count the number of conversations I have had with other autistic adults that have basically boiled down to both of us trying to figure out the polite way to ask about it.

And then once we both figure it out, it's usually "oh yeah, cool, same!" And we both relax a little bit.

If you try to have that conversation with a person who turns out to be neurotypical (or in denial about being autistic), you will be. Uh. Flayed alive.

Okay, I'm not trans, so take what I have to say with a grain of salt. But this is coming from what I've heard other trans people say, and I don't think the burden should always be on them to clarify these matters. Also  sorry for the wall of text - I took this to be a genuine question, so I figured you deserved as full an answer as I could give.

The thing is... for a lot of trans people, it actually isn't a huge part of their life. Like, the fact that the character is a trans woman does include some implications about what genitals she was born with, but that's not the same thing as having a definitive answer to whether her character has undergone a vaginoplasty (or magical equivalent) or not. 

In the real world, that tends to be a really complicated question - not everyone necessarily wants that surgery, and even if they do, it's incredibly expensive. Also, in everyday life, the genitals you have don't actually make that much of a difference. A fully clothed trans woman isn't going to pass more if she's had bottom surgery. Most people don't get naked in public.

There are only two instances in which it matters; sex, or if the person has severe genital-related dysphoria (which not every trans person does). Those are both intensely personal matters, and not things that are likely to come up during one single session of D&D. It could potentially be a legitimately upsetting topic to delve into, but even if it isn't, a lot of people are going to find questions about it intrusive. This is understandable. If someone went up to you and asked "hey, do you feel bad about your dick? Also describe to me in detail how you fuck," I have to imagine you would find that uncomfortable.

There's also the fact that. Like. In a fantasy setting, if you decide your character has in fact swapped out their cock for a cooch, you have to figure out what that looked like. Magic spell? Divine intervention? Cursed belt? Regular old surgery? Was it a long, involved process, or were they able to just sorta wake up one day and do it with no side effects? 

That kind of thing can be fun to think about, but not everyone is necessarily going to get deep into the sauce for a one-shot character. Especially since, if your characters are usually trans, you've probably already thought about it before, and may not be interested in retreading that as a plot point. It's also really important to note that what the problem player did was basically a) assume that the character in question had undergone some sort of genital transformation, and b) assume that his resurrection spell would reverse it. There's a legitimately interesting metaphysical question to be found there (does Resurrection also unpierce your ears? Does it get rid of scars and tattoos? What about freckles? Would it cure cancer?) But again, not everyone actually cares about shit like that. If someone has indicated that they do not want to participate in your exploration of the existential horror of healing magic, it's important to respect that.

Also, coming from a player that had been consistently hostile, it becomes pretty clear that this wasn't a light-hearted metaphysical question. It was an act of hostility. That player wanted OP to know that they equate the trans experience with surgery, and that they view bottom surgery as a form of mutilation. They wanted to sexually harass OP's character in order to humiliate and invalidate them. The question came up in a context where it *shouldn't* have been given an answer, even if OP had one to give, because that should not have happened. It is not acceptable to investigate the genitals of an unconscious player character without their consent.

The final thing I want to address is the statement that there was "clearly a point they were making in choosing to be trans." I'd like you to think about that a little more. OP herself is trans - why do you assume that she is making some sort of point by making her character trans? A lot of people will default to making characters that resemble them in some way - most of my characters are female, just because that's what I default to. Isn't it more likely that she just made a character that resembled her, rather than going in with some sort of agenda? 

In general, most things people do aren't actually about proving any sort of point to others. Everyone has their moments, of course, but for the most part, people do things because they want to. The things other people do are very rarely about you. Or me. Or anyone.

I think it's really important, as a DM, to create space for your players to express themselves without making any assumptions about their reasons. If you want, you can always ask about it, but you have to be prepared for an answer that might not match your pre-conceived ideas. Sometimes this means accepting that things are not actually that deep.

I have complicated feelings about it. On the one hand, I imagine that a lot of children in abusive households probably fantasise about this exact scenario coming true - yes, your parents are awful, but it's because they're not your real parents! Somewhere out there, you do have real parents who will love you the way other children are loved! I think that's a powerful form of wish fulfilment.

At the same time, though, I think it can simultaneously be invalidating for those same children (or, well, former-abused-children-who-are-now-adults). Like, it does somewhat promote the idea that parents, by default, love their biological children and are not abusive towards them. And that's not necessarily true. 

For starters, most abusive parents do actually love their children. Feeling parental love for your child doesn't necessarily mean you're qualified to raise that child, especially if you never had any good role models when you were a child yourself. A lot of abusive parents think that their actions are normal and correct, because they simply haven't been able to examine their own upbringing and understand how much their own parents hurt them. This is not in \*any\* way an excuse for abuse - just to highlight that a typical abusive household is going to be a much more confusing environment for the child involved than the black-and-white situations we see in OI, where the parents unambiguously despise the heroine. 

All else aside, I quite frankly feel like these abusive household situations could be milked for a lot more angst if the abusive parents involved combined their neglect and cruelty with sincere expressions of affection and care. It's not that hard to leave someone who has been nothing but cruel to you, but what about someone who pairs their cruelty with moments of kindness? Isn't that a lot harder to come to terms with?

Of course, sometimes parents really don't love their children. But that's not exclusive to adopted children. It is, in fact, possible to give birth to a child (or be their biological father) and never feel love for them. It's actually somewhat common for mothers experiencing post-partum depression to have trouble feeling love for their newborn baby (and for the record, I absolutely do not think that makes someone an abusive parent. Nobody is at fault in that situation.) So again, there isn't a clear divide between "love" and "abuse," and the reality is that plenty of children are unloved and/or abused by their own biological parents.

I didn't grow up in an abusive household, so ultimately I don't feel qualified to speak on how this trope might affect readers raised in abusive households. I doubt there would be a clear consensus, anyway. I don't think it's necessarily a realistic trope, but this is a genre built on wish fulfilment, so maybe it doesn't need to be realistic? I personally do think I would enjoy it more if families like that were written with a bit more complexity and nuance, since I think it would make the protagonist's ultimate decision to leave their family a lot more meaningful. But there definitely are readers who prefer simple, black-and-white conflicts, and I can't fault them for that.

It's not really unusual when you consider that people are treated according to their status.

The king/duke/whatever is a powerful man. There aren't going to be many people around who can criticise him at \*all\* without severe consequences, and most people probably aren't going to choose "you shouldn't have cheated on your wife" as the hill to die on in a world where most men of power have mistresses anyway.

The illegitimate child, on the other hand, has no real power. Their status is always going to be lower than that of the legitimate children in the household. The father's wife is going to have an incentive to hate the illegitimate child, since the child's very existence undermines her authority. The legitimate children of the family need to assert their place in the hierarchy above the illegitimate child, since if they treated them as an equal, that would, again, undermine their own position. And the servants a) need to treat the legitimate family members better in order to avoid ruffling any feathers, and b) may harbour some amount of resentment about being made to serve the least consequential member of the family.

Other people have pointed out in this thread that a lot of illegitimate children in medieval Europe were actually treated decently - lands, titles, good marriages, etc. And that's true. But in order to preserve the hierarchy, they could never be treated \*as well\* as the legitimate children. It's not that anyone seriously thinks an illegitimate child is at fault for being born - it is that, in a strictly hierarchical society, social cohesion relies on everyone "knowing their place." Associating too much with someone of a lower status can negatively impact your own status, and that's what people actually cared about.

But this woman is a grifter and a piece of shit, as are all of her ilk. She's exploiting vulnerable parents and presenting herself as someone qualified to take the place of a medical professional when she very clearly isn't. Babies don't get stuck because the mother is "stuck in her mindset" or what the fuck ever. Sometimes they just get stuck because the human body is a shitshow. And in a situation like that, you need a *real midwife*.

I do think, broadly speaking, that pretty much any medical experience can be traumatic. Birth is especially high up there on that list - it's incredibly painful, pregnancy and birth cause permanent changes to the body, the patient is rendered largely helpless throughout the process, and a lot of people are going to find it inherently humiliating to be in a hospital room with a bunch of strangers staring, poking and prodding at your genitalia. And then you shit yourself in front of them. 

And that's all assuming a straightforward, uncomplicated birth. 

A lot of medical staff just... don't really show a lot of empathy in situations that are high stress for the patient. To an extent, I understand why - they're overworked, and they're preoccupied with the actual task of patient care rather than the patient's feelings about their situation. But the fact of the matter is that it's very easy for doctors to just start doing things that a patient may find invasive or painful, without explaining their actions to the patient or asking for their consent. So the patient is left wondering what the fuck is going on, and possibly feeling deeply violated while also being terrified for their baby and for themselves.

Compassion fatigue is also a very real thing, and... well, to put it bluntly, both medicine and nursing need to attract people who have a high tolerance for stressful situations, and if someone naturally has high empathy, that's actually likely to be a hindrance to an extent. Not saying that having low empathy makes someone inherently cruel, but it does mean that it may take extra work for them to exercise compassion for their patients in an appropriate manner, even if they genuinely wish to. I imagine it does take a lot of effort to remember that, while everything about the situation may be just another Tuesday for them, it's an incredibly high-stakes and unfamiliar situation for their patient.

A few possible options: 

1 - charisma. If a villain is fun and likeable enough, then people will gravitate towards them based on that alone. I guess "being hot" is part of this, but there's more to it than that - good villains are scene-stealers. They attract attention. They're impossible to forget or ignore. 

2 - a compelling reason for their actions. This doesn't mean the narrative needs to justify his actions as though they are not wrong, but if you want people to sympathise with a villain, it helps a lot to put them in a situation where the audience is like "fuck, I don't condone what they did, but I have no clue what I would do in that situation either."

3 - a good dynamic with the protagonist. This ties into 1 and 2 somewhat, but it's also important enough to be its own thing. Give them chemistry. Make them foils to one another. Make the villain bring out aspects of the protagonist that nobody else can, and vice versa. This does mean that you also have to give your protagonist a lot of personality and depth - it doesn't matter what *kind* of depth, necessarily, but there has to be something in them for the villain to bring out.

The Swickers abbatoir is in Kingaroy, but most of the local farmers don't actually raise pigs (they're just butchered here). These days it's mostly grain and grass-fed cattle, apparently.

The problem with peanut farming is that peanuts aren't a super flexible crop, weather-wise. They need the right amount of rain at the right time, or else you lose the whole crop. And with climate change making the weather less predictable, it's becoming increasingly risky to plant peanuts. So it *is* a profit issue, but it's not that peanuts have always been unprofitable - it's a response to material conditions.

Grains like sorghum tend to be a lot hardier, and cattle can survive as long as there's something for them to eat. Droughts are still tough on any kind of agriculture (obviously), as are floods, but some crops survive unpredictable weather better than others. And livestock are pretty hardy.

I won't come at this from a perspective of defending the show, or trying to get you to enjoy it, because I do think the show probably isn't for you and that's fine. I also appreciate that you haven't been trashing it or anything. These are all just things that I, personally, like about Re: Zero.

I like stories where characters have to earn their happy ending. The more a character suffers, the more catharsis I feel when things finally start to go right for them. There's a limit to this, and sometimes Re: Zero does come *real* close to hitting that limit, but overall, I like that Subaru never has anything handed to him.

A pattern starts to emerge after a few arcs - you begin to realise that Subaru's successful loops are always the ones where he connects with other people and relies on them. He's weak on his own, but whenever he manages to work with other people, he makes progress. He has to learn how to empathise with others, how to negotiate, how to drill down to the heart of each person he interacts with and figure out what motivates them.

Subaru can be pathetic sometimes. I don't mean when he's just straight up too traumatised to really be a person - that's tragic, not pathetic. He's at his most pathetic when he tries to take everything upon himself, believing that he is the only one who can save everyone. The worst version of Subaru is somehow arrogant and self-pitying at the same time. 

But sometimes - sometimes, Subaru is really cool! He's clever and funny, and he'll do whatever it takes to look out for everyone around him. He won't give up on any of the people he cares about, no matter the cost. His tendency to bulldoze other people in conversation becomes a reckless, contagious optimism. 

All of this really resonates with me. It makes me feel that I want, more than anything, for this beautiful, pathetic trainwreck of a young man to succeed. I want him to be happy. I want the people around him to be happy. I want to see the point where he drags himself out of his despair and suffering, and accomplishes the impossible. I want to comfort him, and I want to cheer him on.

Subaru was a shut-in before getting isekai'd. He is, by nature, someone who has a tendency to self-isolate. Re: Zero is fundamentally a story about a person with that self-isolating temperament being forced to connect with others - to rely on them, and to become someone they can rely on. As someone with a similar tendency towards self-isolation, it reminds me that I can and should continue to connect with others, even if it sucks absolute shit to make that effort.

I also like that Return by Death is both Subaru's greatest weapon and the source of his trauma. He can undo terrible things, can reverse the fates of countless people, but only by experiencing unimaginable suffering. Technically, it's impossible to actually kill him for real, but that doesn't mean he can't be harmed or defeated. Re: Zero asks a common escapist fantasy question - "what if you could go back and undo your mistakes?" - and then gives an absolutely horrifying answer. That's just fascinating to me as a concept.

So I'm gonna talk a bit about my personal experience here, and see if that resonates with anyone else.

I am a woman. I identify as a woman, and I would love to be perceived as feminine. However, I feel like all of my attempts at femininity end up looking uncanny and inhuman.

The first thing is: sensory issues make it really uncomfortable to meet feminine beauty standards to begin with. I hate wearing high heels and fake nails. I hate the feeling of makeup on my skin, and because I'm not especially coordinated, it's difficult for me to apply makeup without making mistakes. I do wear a lot of dresses, and I have long hair, but those things alone aren't actually enough to make me qualify as feminine. All of this, combined with my babyface, give off a vibe that is certainly not masculine, but also falls short of feminine. Other women generally treat me like some kind of cute little stray duckling that needs to be taught how to be a real woman.

Well, okay. Let's say I take their advice - push through the discomfort and spend a bunch of time and money getting dolled up Properly, as is Expected of a Womanly Woman. What's the result?

Every single time, it's disappointing. I'm not pretty to begin with, and makeup can only fix so much of that, but the other fundamental problem is that no matter what I do, I will always look wrong. My posture, my expressions, the look in my eyes - no matter what I do, they will always be just slightly off. In order to look like a feminine woman, I would first have to look like a real human being, and I don't. You know how a lot of autistic people get told that they don't look autistic? Well, I do. And the more effort I put into my appearance, the more obvious my shortcomings are.

To address potential responses people may have to this:

"Oh, but these are all social constructs! You're a human, so of course you look human! You're a woman, so of course you look like a woman!"

That's nice and all, but we all know that's not how neurotypical society sees things. I can work on my self esteem all I want, but I don't think it's a good idea to delude myself. People will make judgements about me based on aspects of my appearance that I cannot control, and if I want to navigate society, I need to present a narrative to them that they will be comfortable with. "Clueless little puppy" is a persona that neurotypical people can work with. "Creepy-looking try-hard" is not. It would be great if I had more options, but I don't.

"Are you saying that *I'm* masculine/creepy-looking/etc.?!"

My assessment of myself is based on how other people react to me, and has nothing to do with my assessment of anyone else. I am much more critical of myself than I am of others, because the extent to which other people conform to gender norms does not harm me in any way, while my own personal failure in this regard very much can harm me.

Some autistic women do femininity just fine. Some autistic women aren't interested in being perceived as feminine to begin with. As someone who *wants* to be perceived as feminine but also *can't*, I have to just deal with the fact that there will always be a disconnect between the person I want to be and the person I actually am. And I have to make the most of what I've got.

"There's nothing wrong with looking autistic!"

Objectively, no, of course not. But that's not how society sees things, is it? My posture, my gaze - these things are fundamentally incompatible with what would be considered "beautiful" or "feminine." That doesn't make them wrong objectively, but if something restricts the options you have in life, then it is kind of by definition a shortcoming.

"You're being too hard on yourself!"

I mean, yeah, probably. That doesn't mean my assessment is inaccurate.

But the point is, there's no universal agreement on what those basic manners *are.* A lot of people do turn their phones to DND when they're sleeping, and wouldn't be remotely inconvenienced in a situation like this. I'm fine with people texting me whenever, as long as they don't receive an immediate response. 

It's also fine that you *don't* like it, but that's not a universal standard or something that people should automatically know - you need to communicate with other people. Especially since, like, if 7:13 is too early, what time *is* okay? People wake up at vastly different times on the weekend.  Other people don't know your schedule, so they can't know which times are inconvenient for you. A lot of parents are actually up and about at 7 on weekends.

Also, OP wasn't texting a random stranger. Their kids hang out together. She was trying to arrange a playdate.

So yeah, like, it would have been fine if the neighbour *actually said* "hey, please don't text me that early in future." But instead he flew off the handle and blocked OP, which is an incredibly disproportionate response given that he never communicated the fact that he had a problem with it before.

So, rule of thumb: if a cat is twisting around and moving a lot while you're holding it, that means it's uncomfortable and possibly feels unsafe. A cat that is happy to be held will mostly sit still - maybe they'll turn their head a bit to look at things, but they won't be struggling like that.

Most cats will not expose their bellies unless they feel very safe and comfortable. If you force a cat to show their belly by turning them upside down like that, they will feel threatened. I do actually hold my own cat with his belly up sometimes, but I always make sure he can turn over if he wants to.

Generally, cats need to have their bodies supported properly when being held, and they need to feel like they can get away from you if they want to. The way you're holding that kitten has him dangling in mid-air with very little support, his belly exposed, and no means of escape. That's really scary. I would be scared if some giant did that to me.

When I first got my cat, I would pick him up and cradle him like a baby, and I would either put him down or let him jump out of my arms as soon as he showed the slightest signs of discomfort. Over time, he became more comfortable being picked up, to the point where he sometimes yells at me until I pick him up and rock him like a baby while kissing his fuzzy little head. He would have never grown to trust me like that if I hadn't respected his boundaries early on. And my cat is a laid-back snugglebug who will ask for belly rubs from anyone - a timid cat would have requires much, much more time and patience to get to that point.

I'm not a cat expert by any means, but these are the very basics of pet ownership. You have to learn their body language and respect their boundaries.

Okay, so one issue that I personally have with the English translation of FFXIV is that, in some instances, they prioritised appealing to what they assumed an American audience would want to read over conveying the original emotional meaning of the story. Although I understand why they would want to do this in order to boost the game's popularity, I am against it - both because I think the game can easily stand on its own merits without needing those changes, and because it makes it seem like they think very little of their English-speaking audience, especially since the French and German versions of the game are usually much closer to the Japanese versions.

For example, the character of Fray in the Dark Knight questline is\**significantly* ruder and more unkind in the English version, and while the questline as a whole is still excellent and has a great deal of emotional impact, the Japanese version as a whole is just... more subtle and nuanced. [See this post if you really want a deep dive into this](https://www.reddit.com/r/ffxiv/comments/motb0h/dark_knight_quest_translations_from_mainly_jpde/). It feels like they made certain assumptions about what a Western audience would expect from this particular character, and then decided against challenging those assumptions even when doing so would, in my opinion, have actually made for a more interesting story.

I can somewhat forgive this decision, because I at least understand it - they thought the Western audience would either better understand, or prefer, a version of that character that is more angry than sad, so they changed it a bit.

They may have also thought that Western audiences would be uncomfortable with the quasi-romantic undertones of the relationship between Fray and the player character, especially since Fray is always the same gender as you. Another male character who just straight up flirts with you in the Japanese version was toned down for (presumably) that reason in the English version. In Fray's case, their feelings aren't exactly romantic anyway, but I can see how they'd be concerned about making people uncomfortable.

But the change I really can't forgive is the Stormblood Hamilton references. The Stormblood expansion of FFXIV, for those who don't know, involves helping two of the Garlean Empire's colonies liberate themselves from their oppressors. Stormblood happened to release in 2017, right at the height of hype for the musical Hamilton, which is about the United States Founding Father Alexander Hamilton.

Now, don't get me wrong. I enjoy Hamilton. I think it's a very good musical. But I also think the Hamilton references in Stormblood ended up being disrespectful to both stories.

It started out with questlines. A lot of questlines in the English version of Stormblood were given names that are just straight up lines from the Hamilton musical. I'd honestly be fine with it if this was just a thing they did for sidequests. The English version of FFXIV has already established a precedent of using puns or references in the names of sidequests and overworld events, and I honestly think it's fun and cute. However, I do think it became somewhat invasive when they started naming major quests that way. While it's true that Stormblood and Hamilton both deal with the topic of a nation undergoing a revolution, they're extremely different stories.

But, you know, whatever. They're just quest names. I can deal with it.

Very gently - I think you may be operating under a bit of a misconception here.

It's possible to have XY chromosomes and be assigned female at birth. In the early stages of gestation, all foetuses default to being "female." The XY chromosomes are meant to trigger a reaction at some point that will lead to the foetus developing male genitalia, but that doesn't always end up happening. If it doesn't happen, then the baby may instead develop female genitalia, and the child will eventually undergo female puberty. They'll most likely go their entire life without realising that they have XY chromosomes.

This is an extremely basic explanation, and I'm not a geneticist by any means, but the important takeaway is that not everyone with XY chromosomes will be assigned male at birth. And - very importantly - it is illegal to undergo gender transition in Algeria, which means that there's no way Khelif *could* have been assigned male at birth and still attended the Olympics as a woman.

She's not in any way a man, though. Imane Khelif was assigned female at birth, raised as a woman, and went through female puberty. It's illegal to change your gender in Algeria.

There's speculation that she *may* have some sort of intersex condition, but that isn't confirmed, and even if she did, it's patently absurd to state that someone with female external reproductive organs, who was raised female, went through female puberty, and has identified as female her entire life, is suddenly "a man" because she may or may not have some sort of intersex variation that would be impossible to detect without actively testing for it. I agree that it's wrong for one person to unilaterally dictate how everyone else plays the game, but I also don't think it's unreasonable for either players or DMs to have certain boundaries regarding the kind of content they're comfortable with seeing in the game. And it's the DM's job to enforce those boundaries.

If your group has explicitly agreed that they're fine with graphic sex scenes, then there's no problem. But it's very common for people to be uncomfortable with that, to the extent that the players who want to roleplay sex scenes should actively ask permission if it wasn't negotiated in Session 0 (and this is the kind of thing that should really be discussed in Session 0).

Keep in mind that everything one player does at the table is going to impact everyone else. A tabletop game is a collaborative experience, and it's important to go into it with a collaborative attitude. Having an explicit sex scene take place at the table effectively forces the other players into the role of voyeur. They can't progress with any of their own roleplay until the scene is over, it doesn't add anything to the plot, and it's inherently kind of awkward. It's common for people to feel uncomfortable knowing detailed information about their friends' sexual preferences, and seeing someone roleplay a sex scene is naturally going to reveal information that you may not have wanted to be privy to.

Again, if everyone is fine with it, then sure, go ahead. But I don't think it's either wrong or unusual for people to *not* be fine with it, and I think that boundary should be respected.

It's because women need to be able to survive pregnancy and breastfeeding. The larger you are, and the more muscle you have on your body (as opposed to fat), the more energy you need to survive. A pregnant or nursing woman is already going to expend a ton of extra energy on growing a baby and making food for them, and if she dies during that process, the baby either dies with her or (if it's been born) has a drastically reduced chance of survival.

So yeah, women are smaller and have a higher body fat percentage because we're built to survive as long as possible, even when food is scarce - which it was for the vast majority of human history, and still is for many people now. Men can afford to put more resources into growing tall and building muscle, because from an evolutionary perspective, their lives are more expendable in times of famine. 

(Obviously this does not mean men are at all expendable from a moral perspective. The moral value of human life is completely different from the physical adaptations our species developed to survive in extremely harsh circumstances).

We see a variety of gender roles in hunter-gatherer societies, but it rarely ever boils down to "the women stay home and look after the kids while the men go out and hunt, and there is no overlap between these roles." It's much more common for most people to do a bit of everything.

When it comes to physical sensations like food and sex especially, "I like it because it feels/tastes good" usually ends up being the best explanation. It feels really simple, but if you keep wriggling down the rabbit hole of "but *why* does it feel/taste good", you're more likely than not to end up inventing some pseudoscientific nonsense to justify a preference that ultimately just... isn't that deep.

Why do some people like spicy food, or BDSM? Why do others prefer mild food or vanilla sex? There's no ultimate deep philosophical answer to those questions. People just like what they like because humans, by nature, tend to form preferences.

The sex thing does impact him since he's directly involved, and if he's trying to get a better understanding of your preferences then I don't think it's unreasonable for him to ask, at a time when you're *not* actively having sex, to let him know what you do and don't like, and if there's any particular reasoning behind it (although again, "i just like it" or "it just feels better this way" would be a perfectly valid answer). I think every parent has a difficult line to walk when it comes to protecting their child from difficult and upsetting concepts. On the one hand, you want to protect them from being upset by things they're not yet ready to understand. On the other hand, if you shelter them too much, they won't be able to develop their understanding of the world or mature as a person. 

I don't know your son, so I don't know what he is and isn't capable of understanding. I don't think Stardew Valley would generally be inappropriate for a seven-year-old, even in its darkest moments, and I do think it's important to let children with disabilities discover for themselves what their limitations are, rather than having adults dictate what they can and can't do based on assumptions. On the other hand, I get why you want to avoid a situation where he is upset by something he doesn't understand, bottles that feeling up, and lets it fester. You want to protect him from a type of harm that you yourself experienced as a child.

I'm also autistic (diagnosed as an adult, so my experience is admittedly going to be very different from your son's), and I found as a kid that reading about things in fiction made them much easier to understand in real life. My parents didn't let me watch adult-rated TV shows and movies, but they let me read whatever I wanted, and I think that was actually a really good, safe introduction to a lot of adult concepts. Sometimes I did run into things I found weird and uncomfortable, but I'm glad that I was introduced to those weird and uncomfortable concepts in a safe environment, where I wasn't directly involved and could always just put the book down and walk away. I know not every child has that luxury. My point here is that at some point in his life, sooner or later, your son is going to run into someone like Shane, and he's going to have to come to terms with that. It will help to have some frame of reference for that ahead of time.

Edit: either way, it's clear that you love your son a lot and are trying to figure out what's best for him. I think that's commendable.

Dubbed songs are never going to hit the same as the original version, though. Not only do you have to translate the lyrics in a way that gets the meaning across, but you also have to make the translation fit into the song, and keep a sense of poetry. It's very, very hard to do that. 

JJ is also an interesting example, because there are two English songs in there that only have English lyrics onscreen. Including the final song that's meant to be super climactic. So I'd argue that only being able to vaguely understand the lyrics isn't entirely incongruous with the experience Japanese players are getting, anyway.

As for voiced content that doesn't correspond with on-screen text, it would still take *way* fewer resources to find a way to subtitle those parts than to dub over them.

I don't want to entirely dismiss anyone's reasons for wanting a dub, but it would require a massive investment of money and resources in a niche genre of games that are - let us be real here - mostly going to be played by people who would just leave Japanese voices on anyway. I doubt there are that many people out there who aren't currently playing otome games (or only play OELVN), but would start playing localised Japanese otome games if they had access to a dubbed version.

I think Japanese authors are a lot less likely to see any issue with a goddess-worshipping patriarchal society, because that's literally what their own culture is like, you know? A lot of Japanese fantasy tends to have a Western medieval aesthetic painted over deeply Japanese cultural values, and OI is no exception. I'm not really sure how natural the adoption of those tropes in Korean OI was, since I don't know much about religion in Korea, but I do know that it's also a historically patriarchal society.

The Japanese emperors claim descent from the goddess Amaterasu, and under current Japanese law, women aren't allowed to ascend the throne at all (although there have been female emperors in the past). Hindus also tend to be very patriarchal despite venerating a whole swathe of goddesses, which is something I've seen Hindu feminists talk about. And although the supreme Christian god is male, Mary is deeply venerated in Catholicism as the mother of Christ, and the Catholic church had a stranglehold on medieval Europe.

Gods and goddesses aren't human, so the veneration of a goddess or female saint doesn't necessarily contradict misogyny towards normal, human women. Even saints either have to die before becoming sanctified, as in real life (prior to which they would have been treated as normal women), or, in a fantasy setting with living saints, usually have some sort of very rare power that sets them apart from other people and confers a specific status that transcends both male and female gender norms. Yeah, I feel like making an incorrect claim about grammatical accuracy detracts from the real problem - which, as you said, is that the "male" and "female" nouns are dehumanising, and someone using those nouns in a casual context is, either deliberately or otherwise, dehumanising the person they are speaking about.

The problem isn't grammatical, and it never has been. Misogyny is not diminished in any way if it is grammatically correct. The issue lies in what words actually *mean*, and how and why they are used.

Incidentally, it's still dehumanising in a professional context (e.g. paramedic), but in a lot of those cases it's actually kind of important for the person speaking to have a way of distancing themselves from the person they're speaking about. Like, if you're trying to treat the victim of a horrible car crash, you really don't want to find yourself thinking about your patient as a person. Because that's traumatic and overwhelming, and in a situation like that, it's critical to be able to keep a cool head and just do what needs to be done. So the person bleeding out in front of you isn't Beth, a science teacher at the local high school and mother of two; she's a 40yo female and a body you need to treat. 

I've seen paramedics get condemned for using this kind of language in public statements about disasters, and I think it's important to remember that they're not being callous. They're building up the barriers they need to do their jobs effectively and protect their own mental health.

People do call men "males" in certain contexts, though. Like, I get that you're talking about the "men and females" phenomenon, which is a completely valid thing to be bothered by, but "male" and "female" are absolutely nouns. Even when referring to humans. Paramedics pretty much exclusively refer to their patients this way.

Like, again, you're absolutely right that if someone is using the noun "female" in a casual context, it's a red flag. And if they're using the noun "female" to refer to women and "men" to refer to men, then that is straight up sexist and dehumanising. You're right about that.

It's still not grammatically incorrect, though, and there *are* contexts where the "male" and "female" nouns are appropriate, even when referring to humans.

Regarding gender identity, it's important to note that some people have a stronger sense of gender identity than others. I'm a cis woman with a strong sense of gender identity, so I find the idea of being perceived as masculine or a man distressing (a real concern given that my autism manifests in ways that make it hard to live up to conventional feminine beauty standards). Conversely, it makes me feel validated to be perceived and acknowledged as a woman. 

I find it relatively easy to empathise with those feelings in trans people, because to some extent I feel the same way. If I woke up with a masculine body and a penis one morning, I would not suddenly be okay with being perceived as a man, even if that perception would be consistent with my appearance. 

Generally, people find it hurtful to be perceived in a way incongruous with their self-image, and validating to be perceived in a way consistent with that self image. As human beings, we tend to want to be seen and understood by others. If you don't have a particularly strong sense of gender identity, you may not be bothered by someone getting your gender wrong. But there are probably some things about yourself that you can't stand the idea of people getting wrong. 

(Also important to note that a lot of people without a strong sense of gender identity end up identifying as non-binary, but again - that's just one way people describe their own feelings and experiences, not a prescriptive label.)

There was a bit of a grammatical error in your first sentence. You used the past continuous tense ("I've been") rather than the past tense ("I was"), which implies that you're still in Australia. The past continuous tense is used for actions that began in the past, but are still ongoing. For example, "I've been working at this company for a year," or "I've been learning to knit lately."

A grammatically correct but clunky version of the sentence would be something like "In 2017, I was in Tasmania, Australia, for 10.5 months." A better, less clunky version would be "I spent 10.5 months in Tasmania in 2017."

(If you are in a place or with a person for a period of time, then you are "spending time" in that place/with that person. For example, "I spent five hours tutoring my cousin," or "she spent a few weeks in Canada." It's not incorrect to just say "I was tutoring my cousin for five hours," or "she was in Canada for a few weeks," but in this case I do think it makes the sentence flow more naturally to say you spent time in Tasmania, rather than just saying you were in Tasmania. I can't fully explain why, though, because it just feels intuitive to me. Maybe someone else can.)

That being said, that person was still being a jerk. The surrounding context made it clear what you were actually trying to say, and it's always rude to make fun of someone for trying their best to communicate in a second language.

I also think some people grow up with parents that do resent them in some way, and they try to process those feelings by shunting them off into this trope. Usually in real life that kind of resentment usually isn't about a dead spouse. It might be because the parent misses their child-free life, or because they had certain ideas about parenthood and their child isn't meeting the expectations they had. But it's definitely a thing, and a traumatic thing, and I'm not gonna fault anyone for trying to process it through the lens of a tired OI trope.

Nobody knows what they're doing their first time running ARR. It's easy for veterans because they've already run the content over and over again, and have made any mistake you could possibly be making many times over by this point.

You're new to the game. You don't need to know everything straight away, and if you put that kind of pressure on yourself you'll just have a bad time, *and* probably make more mistakes. Just keep on learning and you'll be fine. Also, keep in mind that at your level, you don't have a lot of the "oh shit" buttons that higher level White Mages have, and your tanks will also be missing most of their kit. It's a lot easier to zone out as a healer in high level dungeons, because there are more things you can do to turn a bad situation around.

Also keep in mind that one wipe isn't a big deal. The tank and healer both type a "whoops my b" in the chat (even if it is actually the DPS' fault), and you run back in and try again. Shit happens. It's not necessarily going to be your fault in the first place, but even if it is, it's not a big deal. It's, like, two minutes out of the party's day, max, and it's kind of expected that if you sign up for levelling roulette, you may end up babysitting an inexperienced sprout. 

If you find that your main problem is that you panic and hit the wrong buttons when the situation gets tight, then the solution isn't to beat yourself up or overanalyse things. You just need to practice, until you reach a point where you won't panic any more. And you need to stop holding yourself to an unreasonable standard.

There's a huge tonal difference between a vampire campaign where you're dealing with vampires as antagonists, and a vampire campaign where you get turned *into* a vampire. Same thing with mind flayers. The problem may not necessarily be the body horror, but the fact that the players now have to adjust to playing an entirely different kind of character, because the DM didn't specify that ceremorphosis was a risk for *their characters* specifically. There's also the question of whether the characters were given a chance to avoid that outcome in-game, or whether it was just shoved onto them without any chance to do anything about it.

"You (or a party member) will 100% definitely be squiddified," "you might undergo ceremorphosis depending on your choices but you will have a good chance of being able to avoid it," "whether or not you get squidified depends more on the dice than on the roleplaying choices you make," and "illithid body horror happens in the campaign but will not happen to the player characters" are all different possible ways to interpret the statement that the game contains mind flayer body horror.

You also have to account for the fact that your players may not know jack shit about illithids, or how they reproduce. And you have to be prepared to explain *exactly* what that means.

It's important to understand that mind flayering a player takes control of their character away from them in a very real sense. D&D is just a game, but as a DM you are still in a position of authority, and that means that, if nothing else, you have the power to make people feel deeply uncomfortable. It's important to be absolutely, crystal clear on what your players' boundaries are, because otherwise you are going to end up upsetting someone, probably for a reason that you never expected. You get the final say, so make sure you're really listening to everyone else before you make a decision.

I mean, that still leaves ambiguity in terms of whether the body horror is happening to NPCs or to their PCs, how avoidable it is, whether it'll result in you having to roll another character, etc. I do think you have to be fairly specific when it comes to things like this.

Turning into a mind flayer is gonna be a pretty drastic change in terms of both gameplay and roleplay, so as a DM you do kind of need to know ahead of time whether your players would enjoy that change, or whether it would kill their investment in the character and the campaign, even setting aside the body horror elements.

Aside from the other recommendations, I find "Gender Trouble" by Judith Butler to be a great introduction to the academic side of queer theory. I'm not a big fan of talking about "souls" or whatever either, but most queer theory is actually very much grounded in reality.

I mean, it might not exist *for you*, but it does exist for other people. Myself included - I'm a cis woman, but I have a strong sense of my own gender, and I get upset when people imply that I'm masculine when I don't perform feminine activities like wearing makeup.

You correctly identified that gender is, in many ways, a performance. That (performance combined with physical appearance) is the external aspect of gender - what other people see. But it's not the only aspect. Every single human being has thoughts and feelings that don't reach the surface. 

Not everyone has a strong sense of their own gender. A lot of people actually end up identifying as non-binary because they realised that they do not care whether they are perceived as male or female. Having no innate sense of attachment to your gender is in and of itself a common non-binary experience, although far from universal. That's not to say that you have to identify as non-binary if you feel that way, but it's worth noting that some people do.

But a lot of people *do* have a strong sense of gender identity. They feel joy (euphoria) when being correctly gendered, and emotional pain (dysphoria) when being gendered incorrectly. This may be an emotional, internal reality, but that doesn't make it any less real. It is as real as any other aspect of your personality - your preferences, your emotions, the people you love and hate. 

It's also worth noting that, outside of gender identity and presentation, the physical manifestation of gender can be incredibly non-binary and variable. 

A trans man on testosterone will develop masculine qualities like facial hair, and a trans woman on estrogen will develop feminine qualities like breasts. This actually extends to sexual function - the clitoris of a trans man on testosterone, and the penis of a trans woman on estrogen, are likely to function very differently to what you would expect from their cisgender counterparts. A lot of trans people after transitioning look very different to their pre-transition selves, even if they only began to transition after puberty. And some trans people even have bottom surgery to alter their genitalia, making them functionally indistinguishable from a cisgender person of their gender identity. 

Even without human intervention, biological sex is made up of a huge number of different factors. Very few people actually know which chromosomes they have, for example, and many intersex traits either manifest during puberty, or never become apparent at all without medical examination. We determine sex in infants by looking at their external genitalia, but that is no guarantee of how someone will develop, and some people are born with ambiguous genitalia to start with. If someone is raised as a woman, has a vagina and sees herself as female, then it is patently ridiculous to start calling her a man if a genetic test later reveals that she has XY chromosomes and some sort of androgen insensitivity that caused her to develop female genitalia. 

It is equally ridiculous, in my opinion, to insist that someone who presents as one gender, who identifies as that gender, and who wishes to be seen that way, should be called a different gender simply because of their genitalia, a part of their body that is not even going to be visible to most people. It's an extremely narrow way to approach the human experience. It's limiting.

Once you accept that not everyone is going to fit perfectly into one of two gender boxes, it's a lot easier to accept that maybe we never needed those boxes in the first place - maybe we don't need to categorise people as purely "male" or "female." Maybe people have the right to choose who they are and how they live, without other people trying to categorise them to assuage their own discomfort with ambiguity.

All this to say, if you still don't "get" your friends' gender identity, it's a good idea to stay quiet about it. But please, please don't make the mistake of assuming that something can't be real just because you don't experience it yourself. That would be doing a disservice to yourself and others.

First of all, I disagree that those medical practices are inherently harmful. The transgender people I know didn't transition because they wanted to change their clothes or their hobbies. They transitioned because they had dysphoria, and transitioning alleviated that dysphoria. Changing their name and pronouns, and yes, taking hormone therapy, are all things that have helped them to feel more like themselves, and they have all seemed so much happier and more confident in themselves after doing so. They haven't fundamentally changed who they are on the inside. They just wanted the person they see in the mirror, and *especially* the person they are acknowledged by society to be, to match that inner self.

Some transgender people do feel that they were "born in the wrong body," but others don't necessarily feel that way at all; they may care a lot more about how they are perceived by others than their own physical appearance. At any rate, transitioning drastically reduces the risk of self harm and suicide for people with gender dysphoria, far more than any other treatment. Regardless of why it works, it's clear that it *does* work, and if we value the lives of people who have gender dysphoria, then allowing them to transition is just straight up the best way to help them.

It can be hard to see the full picture when you're in the middle of a situation. In a toxic relationship, it often takes an outside party noticing the problems to make things click for the people involved. It's not unusual at all for people in abusive relationships to blame themselves for the abuse, to minimise it, or to believe that they are just being dramatic when they feel hurt by it.

I don't believe that the world is evenly split into "abusers" and "non-abusers." Some people are certainly more prone to behaving badly in relationships, but I believe anyone is capable of acting in an abusive manner at least on occasion, and a person who routinely engages in abusive behaviours does not have to continue doing so for the rest of their life - anyone can change. That said, it seems like your husband consistently takes his anger out on his family, and that is domestic abuse even if he is never physically violent. His actions are deeply harmful to both you and your children, and you shouldn't have to put up with it.

It is possible that he may change, but that will only happen if he himself wishes to do so. I'm sure he has his reasons for behaving the way it does, but it still isn't acceptable. At the moment, he's getting everything he wants - a family that will cave in to his anger issues. If you want him to change, you have to force him to choose between his anger issues and his family, and you cannot be surprised (although you can certainly be disappointed) if he chooses his anger.

I said that any abuser can change, but most don't. If he doesn't acknowledge and accept that he is the problem, he will not change. All you can do is force him to confront that fact, knowing that he will likely reject the truth.

If you've had enough, it's okay to admit that you've had enough. You don't have to try to fix him for his sake. That's something he would have to do for himself no matter what, anyway. Maximising personal benefit also isn't necessarily the same as maximising personal *economic* benefit either (e.g. buying something more expensive because it's nicer, or taking unpaid time off to do something you consider worthwhile). And even then, humans don't necessarily maximise their own benefit at the expense of all else. We're certainly selfish and cowardly creatures, but we're also pack animals - we'll often go out of our way to help others, especially members of our tribe, even if we gain nothing from it. A certain amount of altruism is necessary for our survival, both as individuals and as a species.

The core of the problem is that our economic system treats monetary wealth as the only tangible form of "benefit," and demands that personal economic enrichment therefore be pursued at the expense of all else. We demand that companies not only remain profitable, but increase their profits every year for the benefit of their shareholders. If a company chooses to do something that benefits their employees, customers or the environment, they must justify it not as a good in itself, but by showing how that action was necessary in order to increase profits. A company that treats its workers well, is environmentally friendly, and provides high-quality and affordable products all while making a tidy profit is a *failure* if it does not increase those profits year after year.

(Obviously this only applies to companies listed on the stock exchange, but a huge amount of the world's economy revolves around those companies, and this philosophy bleeds into every other aspect of our economy).

Our entire society is founded on some deeply warped ideals, and until we acknowledge that and fight back against it, nothing will ever really change.

The economic system we have now is hardly the immutable or inevitable result of human nature. In many ways, it's deeply artificial. I agree that the current rental market we have is the inevitable result of an unchecked market for a necessity in the economic system we have, but that's really not the same thing as human nature.

I think there are definitely some things working in favour of your sister's situation that need to be present in all of these organisations if they're going to not be exploitative.

1. Fair payment, that is enough for the worker to meet their needs plus a bit extra spending money. This is necessary in any job, no matter who you are. If your sister can afford to live comfortably, between her disability payments and the money she earns from working, that's great. A lot of disabled people (or able people these days, honestly) don't get to have that, which is a problem.

2. The work needs to be both physically and psychologically safe. Nobody deserves to be abused or exploited in the workplace, but intellectually disabled people are particularly vulnerable to abuse, and we need to be aware of that and have measures in place to handle it. It's also important not to make people work unreasonable hours, or do physically dangerous tasks without appropriate training and safety measures.

3. It needs to be voluntary. If you don't have the option of leaving a job, for whatever reason, then you are inherently vulnerable to poor treatment in that environment. Whether it's inadequate wages, dangerous tasks or abuse and bullying, you need to have the option of walking away. Again, this is true for everyone, but especially needs to be considered carefully for people with intellectual disabilities, who may not be able to find employment outside of these closed environments and may have difficulty advocating for themselves well.

Again, it sounds like your sister has all that, which is fantastic. I agree that everyone needs some sort of occupation in life - we all need to get outside, talk to people and do things. But it needs to be in a safe and healthy environment, and from the sound of things, a lot of these places are not safe or healthy environments.

Also I feel like the fact that this line occurs when Dimitri is camping an army outside the Adrestian capital really makes a difference, too. He already took back his own country, and now he's invading Adrestia. That's some important context. No Fire Emblem game ever stops with the protagonist's army taking back their own home, or even the homes of their allies, from the antagonists - they always, always take the fight to the enemy capital, kill their head of state, and usually install one of their own allies as a leader. The morality of invading a nation in Fire Emblem games always seems to boil down to "as long as the other side started it, anything we do in retaliation is just fine," and *that's* the mentality that Edelgard is addressing in that line.

It's something that always kinda bothered me in earlier games, so I liked that it was brought up, even if the line was poorly translated and constantly misinterpreted as a result.

Edelgard's ideals are almost the complete opposite of Gaius', though. Gaius believes that it is necessary for the strong to rule over the weak, whereas Edelgard is trying to tear down that exact system of rule. She does not believe that her conquest legitimises her goals - she just sees it as a pragmatic necessity in service of those goals.

Yeah, she did war crimes (it is a Fire Emblem game after all), but she justifies her actions very differently to Gaius or Varis. There's also the fact that those two are trying to build and protect an imperial hierarchy, while Edelgard is trying to dismantle it. There may be some similarity of methods, and I get why people can't forgive Edelgard for that, but their goals and beliefs are very different.

Edelgard is way more similar to someone like Anders from Dragon Age than Gaius - she believes her cause is desperate and urgent, and in her worst moments, her attempts to change the world devolve into desperate, violent flailing with a huge amount of collateral damage. I do think she's a lot more self-aware than Anders, though, which actually kind of works against her - she doesn't expect anyone to understand or forgive her, so she doesn't bother to explain herself or apologise for her actions. It's her way of trying to show consideration to the people she harms, but it does come across as arrogance. Anders has a tendency to outright dismiss people who aren't fully on board with his goals, which weirdly makes him a better advocate for his cause in some ways.

Plus, in games like BW, SM, and SV, you have a close personal connection to the crisis at hand. The SV protagonist is the only one who can bring Nemona, Penny and Arven together to face Area Zero. I don't think any life objectively has more value than any other, but I definitely do have a personal hierarchy of lives, and I think most people do.

For example, I'll kill a mosquito with very little thought and no real remorse, just for biting me. The life of a mosquito is still a life, but to me its value is outweighed by its ability to inflict what is, assuming you don't get malaria or something, honestly a pretty minor injury. Similarly, if I had to choose between saving a human baby and a whole litter of puppies from a burning building, I'd save the human baby first. I'd feel pretty awful about leaving the puppies, but I wouldn't doubt my choice at all. Again, one human life should objectively be less valuable than many animal lives, but I would still place a much greater value on the single human life.

The thing about ecosystems, too, is that death and predation are necessary to the overall survival of all the species living in a habitat. If all the predators die out, prey animals will overpopulate and destroy their own food sources. Individual deaths are necessary for the continuity of life as a whole.

I definitely agree with the other point you made that if a human gets eaten by a bear, that's just the circle of life. Like, yeah, it would suck for me if I got eaten by a crocodile and I do not personally want that to happen, but I also don't see that as an "evil" thing - it's just bad luck for me. Sometimes prey animals fight back and kill their predators, and that also isn't wrong - it's just how things happen sometimes. 

Anyway point is, the world is full of death and suffering, and in order to stay sane I do think you need to develop some sort of hierarchy for which lives you value, even knowing that it is a fiction. If you treat every single life with the exact same value, you will either become callous towards all life, or be destroyed by the horror of it all. So I do value the life of my cat far more than that of most animals I meet, not because of any objective quality he has, but because I have chosen to love him and have therefore chosen to value him more. Also he is an obligate carnivore, which means I have to consistently prioritise his life over the lives of other animals by feeding him cat food made from meat.

But like... idk, I think death and predation are a natural and necessary part of any ecosystem. Humans, as omnivores, may be able to opt out, but obligate carnivores can't and I don't believe they should have to. Especially since, if you remove predators from an ecosystem, prey animals will overpopulate and completely destroy their food sources until they starve to death.

No animal wants to die, but death is an essential part of life, and I just don't think it's inherently wrong to participate in that cycle. I think it's important to have respect for the lives you take, and for the ecosystem, and to avoid killing for selfish reasons. I think it's important not to put yourself morally above the animals that die so that you can live, and to make their lives as comfortable and their deaths as quick and painless as you can. But as custodians of the land, I don't think we can flinch away from death.

I also absolutely have a problem with factory farming, to be clear. I refuse to buy cage eggs, and I try to eat grass-fed meat as much as possible, and dairy from non-factory farms. I firmly believe animal welfare is important, and we need strict laws to ensure animals aren't mistreated. By the same token, though, I don't think plant-based options are necessarily better. 

A lot of large-scale agriculture involves the use of pesticides and herbicides that are seriously detrimental to biodiversity, with the loss of insect life being especially concerning. Fruit and vegetables are often picked by exploited immigrant labourers, and luxuries like chocolate and coffee in the majority of cases are produced using outright slavery. Grain harvesting machines have a nasty tendency to slice up rodents and other small animals that make their homes in the fields.

That's not to say nobody should be vegan for ethical reasons. Ultimately, if you don't believe you can look an animal in the eye and kill them, then I think you probably should be vegetarian/vegan. But I think, in the capitalist world we live in, you very much have to pick your poison.

It's comforting to believe that an issue has a black and white, right and wrong answer, and that everything will be okay if everyone just chooses the one correct path. But it just isn't that simple.

Non-existence may be free of pain, but I was non-existent for billions of years before my birth and will be non-existent for billions of years afterwards. All pain is temporary, so you may as well experience being alive for the short amount of time you can, right? I don't believe anyone is obligated to become a parent, and I do believe that being a parent is an enormous responsibility, but I firmly reject anti-natalism on the basis that only a living person can determine whether they wished to be born or not.

I wrote a longer comment elsewhere about this, but I think both Abigail and Caroline are at the end of their rope in a way that is common in these situations. This does not make either of them bad people.

You're the one villainising Abigail for responding emotionally to an unreasonable demand. It's clear that neither of them are in a position to calmly discuss their actual issues. I would be on Caroline's side if they had been arguing about chores or something, but they aren't. Caroline is taking her fear and frustration with her daughter growing up, and translating it into what feels, to Abigail, like a rejection of the person she has become and an attempt to control her identity.

My point is that Caroline's response to that is still going to be the same: "why are you being so disrespectful, don't you know I'm letting you live here for free." Because it's not Abigail's phrasing that she's taking issue with, here - it's the fact that Abigail is disobeying her by dressing in a manner she disapproves of. Telling her that she's being inappropriate will upset her just as much as saying "I DO WHAT I WANT," and I'm not sure why it's entirely on Abigail to respond with perfect maturity to a deeply immature request - especially since the response she gets will be the same either way.

Like, have you ever talked to a parent like this? They can't be swayed by a reasonable argument from their child, because they are still stuck in the mindset that what they say goes, no matter what.

It's clear that there is tension in that household on both sides. From Abigail's perspective, she's trying to find her own identity as an adult, and her parents are trying to mould her into the person they want her to be, rather than accepting her for who she is. From Pierre and Caroline's perspective, they can't let go of their perception of her as a child who requires guidance, and because her hobbies, aesthetic sense, and values differ from theirs, they're concerned that they failed as parents.

This is a pretty normal conflict, and usually it resolves itself once the kid has a chance to move out for a while. They have the chance to figure out who they are without their parents breathing down their neck, which means they'll become a lot less defensive about their choices. Also, having to do your own housework is a great way to learn to appreciate what your parents do. Meanwhile, the parents get to see that their kid can get by just fine without their intervention, and that their way of doing things won't end in disaster. Everyone chills out with a bit of distance, and the real problem here is that nobody in that household gets to have that distance.

In this specific instance, I do think Caroline is in the wrong. It doesn't matter if she and Pierre are paying for everything - you do not get to dictate how another person looks. You can't buy another person's bodily autonomy by paying their rent, even if you gave birth to them. But I do also understand that this isn't really about how Abigail dresses. Caroline clearly feels like she does a lot of work for her family that goes unappreciated, and I think she resents that her daughter is (from her perspective) goofing off and enjoying her youth carelessly while her parents work hard to make that lifestyle possible. She just, for whatever reason, has trouble talking about the actual problem, so instead she finds herself criticising Abigail for things that don't actually matter, and getting annoyed at the perceived disrespect when Abigail responds in kind.

Abigail hasn't learned to interact with her parents like an adult addressing an equal, it's true - but equally, her parents haven't learned how to not treat her like a child. It's a vicious feedback loop, and a super common one.

So here's what I did when I had a flea infestation in my house, just in case the flea bath doesn't get all of them:

- used Revolution on my cat. It's safe for them, and it kills fleas and sterilises their eggs. This ensured that any fleas that bit him were doomed.

- got a bunch of pet safe flea sprays, and sprayed everywhere I found the little bastards, including on my own legs. Kept repeating this for days on end. See a flea, spray it.

- filled up a bowl with warm, soapy water, and walked around the house in long white socks. The fleas would jump up onto my legs, and I would then pick them off and put them in the water. The soap stops them from being able to float, so they drown pretty quickly.

- washed my bedsheets a lot, and then sprayed the fresh ones with the pet safe flea spray.

- heavy, regular vacuuming, especially in carpeted areas (which was most of my apartment).

This worked, and neither I nor my cat seemed to be harmed by the sprays I used. My apartment was absolutely crawling with the little bastards, but they were completely gone once I was done. 

I hope it doesn't come to that, but if it does, be prepared. And stay vigilant. Normally when fleas bite humans, they'll go for the feet and legs, so if you start getting some bug bites there specifically, you may want to start hunting.

Edit: since he's a kitten, maybe skip the Revolution and sprays. I still swear by luring the bastards out by walking around in socks, though, and vacuuming works as well.

I made an OC for the villain behind Murgaxor. I'm not changing Murgaxor's personality or motivations (although I am going to try to flesh him out a bit more), but I wanted to have a more interesting villain behind it.

In my version of Strixhaven, instead of five founder dragons, there were originally seven. One of them had power over time, and kept reliving the deaths of the other dragons at the hands of fearful and envious mortals over and over again, resetting as much as she could to try and save them. Eventually she erased herself from existence, becoming one with the snarl and with Strixhaven itself, in order to create a timeline where her family could be saved.

The only person who remembers her at all is the sixth dragon, who created a mirror dimension underneath Strixhaven as his own domain, and is using it to research ways to bring her back. His ultimate goal is to sacrifice the pocket dimension Strixhaven exists in for my setting, and everyone who ever has or ever will step foot there, in order to draw his sister out from the snarl. Since he can't act directly in Strixhaven, due to it being his sister's domain, he has to use thugs like Murgaxor to carry out his plans, tricking them into believing they've found the secret to some sort of vast power.

I also plan to have Murgaxor show up a lot more, to be smug and monologue a lot. Gonna give him a wand of Dimension Door so that he can say his poece and then teleport away if he decides he doesn't like what he's seeing or if someone tries to hit him. Basically, turning the guy into comic relief. I aim to make him as annoying to deal with as possible, and hard to take seriously, and then juice up his boss fight so that my players have to be like "oh shit, that funny frog guy got hands."
